target_audience: Advanced university students with a strong foundation in calculus and linear algebra.

sections.title: Introduction: The Putnam Mindset
sections.content: A brief overview of the Putnam competition: it's not about speed, but about elegant, creative proof construction. We introduce the core philosophy: reduction, symmetry, and parity.
sections.example: Visualize a 'Detective Cat' searching for a hidden pattern in a grid of numbers, turning a complex algebraic expression into a simple geometric symmetry.

sections.title: Strategy 1: The Principle of Extremity
sections.content: Prerequisite: Basic real analysis. We explain how to focus on the 'worst-case' scenario or the boundary of a set. By analyzing the maximum or minimum element, a complex system often collapses into a solvable proof.
sections.example: Imagine a flock of birds flying in a closed space; by looking at the 'outermost bird,' we prove that all birds must eventually be contained within a specific radius.

sections.title: Strategy 2: Combinatorial Invariants and Parity
sections.content: Using graphical visualizations (colored tiles or toggling light switches) to show how certain operations keep a property 'invariant.' This is critical for showing impossibility proofs.
sections.example: A robot navigating a 3D maze: show that the parity of its grid coordinates acts like a color-coded state, preventing it from reaching certain zones regardless of the path taken.

sections.title: Strategy 3: Generating Functions and Recurrence
sections.content: Prerequisite: Series and power functions. We translate a recursive sequence into a power series, allowing us to 'extract' the general term via algebraic manipulation.
sections.example: A 'Magic Fountain' machine where each new layer of water is determined by the two layers below it; representing this as a polynomial makes the water level at the 100th layer easy to calculate.

sections.title: Synthesis & Summary
sections.content: Connecting the dots: How to choose the right tool when facing an unseen problem. Emphasis on structured exploration over brute force.
sections.example: A toolbox metaphor: The student as a mechanic, identifying the 'Problem Engine' and selecting the 'Invariant Wrench' or 'Extremity Hammer' to solve the challenge.
